correctness.rationale: Complete proof for every positive ring size: exact de Bruijn transfer identity and characteristic recurrence; simultaneously conjugated matrices have singular values (λ,λ,1,λ^-2) and (λ^1/2,λ^1/2,λ^-1,0). Product trace inequality settles all targets with ≥4 ones. Exact algebra over the cubic and rational root interval give ||S^m||_2≤1 for m≥3, yielding strict bound for ≤3 ones on n≥25. The 15,250 remaining sparse outputs on n≤24 were exhausted with integer matrices. All four extracted verification programs passed. Direct brute enumeration n≤14 cross-checks, not substitutes for, analytic proof.

originality.rationale: The precise all-length inequality N(y)<N(0^n) for every nonzero cyclic target is not supplied by the inspected prior texts. McIntosh (1993) contains the transfer matrices and qualitative expectation for zero-rich words, not a rigorous global exact cyclic maximum and strict uniqueness theorem. Powley-Stepney imply homogeneous counts only. Jen addresses a distinct infinite-lattice extremal extension statistic. The same-model analysis identified this exact missing comparison and proved it by a simultaneous singular-value argument, a sparse Perron bound and a finite exact boundary. A genuine historical-priority risk is acknowledged; a null search is not taken as proof of novelty.
residual_risks: The 1993 predecessor-growth heuristic and the 1992 state-transition atlas are close antecedents; a historical exact all-length proof may be hard to find by text search.
An uninspected publication could state an abstract matrix-product theorem that implies strict Rule-22 optimality.
Priority was assessed only by same-model review; independently conducted scientific review has not occurred.

value.rationale: The unique global most ambiguous observation and exact largest one-step inverse-fiber for every ring length are natural structural dynamical invariants for a widely studied nonlinear CA. They quantify the maximum information loss in a one-step observation under uniform input. A qualitative zero-rich growth expectation and homogeneous counting do not settle the sharply formulated global extremal problem.
